{{Short description|Substructure of a set theoretical universe}}
{{distinguish|Standard model|text=[[Standard Model]] (particle physics)}}
In [[set theory]], a '''standard model''' for a [[Theory (mathematical logic)|theory]] {{mvar|T}} (in the language of set theory) is a [[model (mathematical logic)|model]] {{mvar|M}} for {{mvar|T}} where the membership relation {{math|∈<sub>''M''</sub>}} is the same as the membership relation {{math|∈}} of a set theoretical [[Universe (mathematics)|universe]] {{mvar|V}} (restricted to the domain of {{mvar|M}}). In other words, {{mvar|M}} is a [[Substructure (mathematics)|substructure]] of {{mvar|V}}. A standard model {{mvar|M}} that satisfies the additional [[Transitive set|transitivity]] condition that {{math|''x'' ∈ ''y'' ∈ ''M''}} implies {{math|''x'' ∈ ''M''}} is a '''standard transitive model''' (or simply a '''transitive model''').

Often, when one talks about a model {{mvar|M}} of set theory, it is assumed that {{mvar|M}} is a '''set model''', i.e. the domain of {{mvar|M}} is a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] in {{mvar|V}}. If the domain of {{mvar|M}} is a [[proper class]], then {{mvar|M}} is a '''class model'''. An [[inner model]] is necessarily a class model, because inner models are required to contain all the [[ordinal number|ordinal]]s of {{mvar|V}}.

== Examples ==
It is difficult to exhibit an explicit set model of ZFC, because the very existence of a set model implies the [[consistency]] of ZFC, which is unprovable within ZFC. However, the universe {{mvar|V}} itself, when equipped with the ordinary set membership relation {{math|∈}}, is an intuitive example of a class model that is standard transitive.{{sfn|Chow|2007|loc=Section 3.2}}

To better illustrate the concepts of "standard" and "transitive", we compare the model {{math|(''V'', ∈)}} with other models [[isomorphic]] to it. An arbitrary isomorphism such as {{math|''f''(''x'') {{=}} {''x'', ∅}<!-- -->}} will usually yield a non-standard class model, since {{math|''x'' ∈ ''y''}} does not imply {{math|{''x'', ∅} ∈ {''y'', ∅}<!-- -->}} in general. To construct a class model that is standard but not transitive, consider a function {{mvar|f}} defined by [[Epsilon-induction|{{math|∈}}-recursion]] as {{math|''f''(''y'') {{=}} {''f''(''x'') {{!}} ''x'' ∈ ''y''} ∪ {∅}<!-- -->}} (essentially, we add {{math|∅}} to every set and to its elements recursively). Denote the [[image (mathematics)|image]] of {{mvar|f}} as {{mvar|M}}. Since {{math|∅}} itself is not in {{mvar|M}}, we have {{math|''x'' ∈ ''y''}} iff {{math|''f''(''x'') ∈ ''f''(''y'')}}, and thus {{math|(''M'', ∈)}} is indeed a standard model, but it is not transitive because {{math|∅ ∈ ''f''(∅) ∈ ''M''}} but {{math|∅}} is not in {{mvar|M}}.{{sfn|Van Dongen|2023}} Essentially, non-standard models have a membership relation different from the universe, and standard non-transitive models have elements with "superfluous" members.

== Absoluteness ==
{{main|Absoluteness (logic)}}
A standard transitive model {{mvar|M}} will in many aspects behave "exactly like {{mvar|V}}". For example, the element that satisfies the [[axiom of empty set]] in {{mvar|M}} will be {{math|∅}}, the empty set of {{mvar|V}}. Similarly, all sets that can be built up from the empty set, the [[axiom of pairing]] and the [[axiom of union]] (i.e., all [[hereditarily finite set]]s) are all the same as their counterparts in {{mvar|V}}. In other words, sentences such as "{{mvar|x}} is the empty set" or "{{math|''x'' {{=}} {∅, {∅}, {∅, {∅}<!-- -->}<!-- -->}} (the [[von Neumann ordinal]] 3)" have the truth value for the same {{mvar|x}}, whether they are interpreted in {{mvar|V}} or any standard transitive model {{mvar|M}}. Such sentences are known as [[Absoluteness (logic)|absolute]] for standard transitive models.

An example of a sentence that is not absolute for standard transitive models is "{{mvar|y}} is the [[power set]] of {{mvar|x}}", which by definition means "for all {{mvar|z}}, {{math|''z'' ∈ ''y''}} if and only if {{math|''z'' ⊆ ''x''}}", or more formally:
:{{math|∀''z'' (''z'' ∈ ''y'' ↔ ∀ ''w'' ∈ ''z'' (''w'' ∈ ''x''))}}.
The qualifier {{math|∀''w'' ∈ ''z''}} means the same thing whether interpreted in {{mvar|V}} or {{mvar|M}}: As long as {{math|''z'' ∈ ''M''}}, transitivity ensures that all elements of {{mvar|z}} must also be in {{mvar|M}}. Therefore, the right hand side of the [[biconditional]] does mean "{{mvar|z}} is a subset of {{mvar|x}}". However, the qualifier {{math|∀''z''}} means {{math|∀''z'' ∈ ''V''}} when interpreted in {{mvar|V}}, but {{math|∀''z'' ∈ ''M''}} when interpreted in {{mvar|M}}. In the latter case, only subsets of {{mvar|x}} that is in {{mvar|M}} is required to be in {{mvar|y}} (in fact, only those subsets could be in {{mvar|y}} due to transitivity). Since an arbitrary subset of {{mvar|x}} is not necessarily in {{mvar|M}} (the [[axiom of separation]] only works for [[definable set]]s), the {{mvar|y}} that satisfies this sentence in {{mvar|M}} may be a proper subset of the power set of {{mvar|x}} in {{mvar|V}} (i.e., the {{mvar|y}} that satisfies this sentence in {{mvar|V}}).{{sfn|Chow|2007|loc=Section 4}}

In general, a sentence is absolute as long as it is equivalent to a formula with only [[bounded quantifier]]s like {{math|∀''w'' ∈ ''z''}}.{{sfn|Kunen|1980|loc=Corollary 3.6, Lemma 3.7}} For example, assuming the [[axiom of regularity]]:
* "{{mvar|x}} is an [[ordinal number]]" is equivalent to "{{mvar|x}} is a [[transitive set]] strictly totally ordered by set membership" and thus is absolute.
* "{{math|''x'' {{=}} ''ω''}} (the first infinite ordinal)" is equivalent to "{{mvar|x}} is an [[Axiom of infinity|inductive set]] containing only {{math|0}} and {{math|''S''(''y'')}} for {{math|''y'' ∈ ''x''}}" and thus is absolute.
On the other hand:
* "{{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}} are [[equinumerous]]" is not absolute, even though "{{mvar|z}} is a bijection between {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}}" is absolute — the existence of {{mvar|z}} is exactly the unbounded qualifier that allows the sentence to be not absolute, as it may be the case that {{mvar|z}} exists in {{mvar|V}}, but is not in {{mvar|M}}. In other words, two sets can be equinumerous in {{mvar|V}}, but not in {{mvar|M}}.
* "{{math|''x'' {{=}} ''ω''<sub>1</sub>}} (the first [[uncountable]] ordinal)" is not absolute, because countability is based on equinumerosity and thus is not absolute. There may exist ordinals that are countable in {{mvar|V}} but uncountable in {{mvar|M}}, and the first such ordinal will "play the role of {{math|''ω''<sub>1</sub>}}" in {{mvar|M}}.
In fact, the downward [[Löwenheim–Skolem theorem]] together with [[Mostowski collapse lemma]] can convert any standard (set) model of [[ZFC]] into a standard transitive model {{mvar|M}} that is itself countable. Every set in {{mvar|M}} must be countable in {{mvar|V}}, but at the same time there must exist sets in {{mvar|M}} that are uncountable in {{mvar|M}}, such as the sets playing the role of {{math|''ω''<sub>1</sub>}} or {{math|𝔓(''ω'')}} (the power set of {{mvar|ω}}). This does not lead to any contradiction because countability is not absolute.{{sfn|Chow|2007|loc=Section 4}}
